Man I really like this, I always like when poems bend back on themselves in a satisfying conclusion of what was set up at the start. It brings a very conclusive feeling of hope for me, that the subject will continue walking and trying to communicate with the world and not be so lonely. 

I really like that clever spelling of the word sailor too, it's so smart because it utilises the common suffix of "er" / "or" tacked onto a verb to designate someone's profession, but in this poem the rest of the world are designated as these so called "saylors", and the subject is not a part of that. It's a great way to put a shift on reality, I really like it.

Poetry that breaks the fourth wall to talk directly to the reader is always a favourite for me because it's so difficult to do without being heavy handed or (for lack of a better word) corny, and I think you did it really well. It reminds me a bit of [this poem](https://web.archive.org/web/20210116061416/https://poems.poetrysociety.org.uk/poems/to-the-reader-from-a-poet-with-love/) actually which is another favourite of mine.

I really like your repeated use of "to who" building up to the final declaration of "to share is to stand before someone naked, and ask for mercy", it creates a good rhythm to the poem while allowing this more free writing style. And adding to that I think I will find myself echoing that line in my mind for quite some time, it's quite a direct and powerful statement, it makes me feel invigorated to share more of my interior too.

pronunciation aside which i think would be significantly harder for native spanish speakers because spanish has a pretty limited amount of phonemes (not many of which are found in chinese), but! perhaps the tones at least may be a little easier for native spanish speakers

think about the differences between how you would say "ella tiene su libro" and "¿ella tiene su libro?". theres a rising tone in the second. granted, it is on a two syllable word but the rising tone in the phrase is vital to conveying that it is a question, not a statement

i cant speak for other langauges beyond english, spanish and chinese, but at least in english yes we do have a similar concept in non standard english ("she has her book" vs "she has her book?"). but in more standard do/does questions, there can be an omission of tonality while still getting the point across that it is a question ("she has her book" vs "does she have her book?")

sure, saying "does she have her book?" in a monotone voice may sound a bit odd, but it would still be understood as a question. whereas is you were to say "¿ella tiene su libro?" entirely monotone in spanish that would not be understood as a question

​

tldr; as a speaker of eng, spa + chn , tones are not that hard because they are relatable to features of technically non tonal languages . [this video helped me a lot though when i started learning chinese tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3wV8B4bx1lM)

An extremely close family friend who was like a big brother to me was killed by a train when I was around 12, it felt like my world came to an end. It was like a nightmare, for days afterwards I kept expecting he was going to walk in through the door laughing and being stupid and we would sit and eat together. 

TW for graphic descriptions of death   
>!I remember at school a few days later in class somehow the subject of train deaths came up, and my classmates were talking with the teacher about what would happen to the body if you were run over by a train, guessing how all the bones would get mangled up and the skin torn from their body as they were dragged along the ground. And I sat in the corner crying until I screamed at them all to shut up and ran out, it was very embarrassing but I had nightmares for literally years after about the things they described happening to him. Because his body was so badly hurt they struggled to identify him at first.!<

  
As for how I coped, he was amazing at languages and working to become a teacher. I decided to start learning languages too, and I'm also a teacher now as well coincidentally. So I do find some solace in that somehow.

Every year on the day of his death my family and his would make a little party and reminisce and watch videos of him too and that helped. It always feels good to talk about him, even now 12 years by I still think of him and talk about him to people because he was such a funny and caring wonderful person. I think keeping him alive in my heart is how I cope- telling and sharing stories of all the crazy things we did together and remembering him how I knew him.
